html:
From 2019 to early 2022 huge swarms of desert locusts swept across East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and South Asia. It was the worst outbreak in 70 years for Kenya and in 25 years for Ethiopia, Somalia and India.

The desert locust is a grasshopper that, after good rains, can switch from living alone to forming swarms of billions that eat their own weight in green plants every day. In 2018 two cyclones dumped rain on the empty sands of southern Arabia. Locusts bred there unchecked, then spread to the Horn of Africa, where more unusual rains in late 2019 let them breed again.

Swarms stripped crops and pasture in places already short of food. The Food and Agriculture Organization led a spraying campaign from the air and ground, but war in Yemen and Somalia made some breeding grounds hard to reach. In 2020 the COVID-19 pandemic slowed the arrival of pesticides and planes.

Scientists link the run of cyclones that started it to a warming Indian Ocean.
